title: Most Items Under Each Budget
statement:
A shop has items with prices prices. You also get a list of shoppers' budgets, budgets.

For each budget budgets[k], find the largest number of items a shopper can pick (each item at most once) so that the total price is at most the budget. Order does not matter, so any subset is allowed. Return the answers in the same order as budgets.

examples.why: With 11 the shopper takes 2 + 3 + 6 = 11, exactly on budget. With 1 nothing fits. With 20 everything fits.
Taking the first item that fits (the 5) gives only 1 item. The three cheap ones give 3.
A budget equal to a total still counts; one unit less loses an item.

hints: To fit the most items into a budget, which items would you always prefer?
The cheapest k items are the best possible set of size k. Sort the prices and take prefix sums.
For each budget, the answer is the number of prefix sums that are ≤ the budget. The prefix sums are increasing, so binary search.

explain.intuition:
If any k items fit within a budget, then the k cheapest items fit too, since swapping an item for a cheaper one never raises the total. So after sorting, the best choice is always a prefix of the sorted prices.

Store the prefix sums once. They only go up, so for each budget, binary search for the last prefix sum that is ≤ the budget. Its length is the answer. That is O(log n) per shopper instead of rescanning the prices.
steps: Build pre[i] = sum of the first i + 1 sorted prices.
For each budget, binary search for the number of entries of pre that are ≤ the budget (upper bound).
Collect the counts in the original budget order.
pitfalls: Taking items in the given order until one does not fit. Cheap items later in the list get missed.
Using a strict lower bound and missing a total that equals the budget exactly.
Sorting the budgets for a two-pointer sweep and forgetting to put answers back in the original order.

solutions.title: Sort, then walk the prices for each budget
solutions.idea: Sort once; for each budget add the cheapest prices until the next one does not fit.

solutions.title: Prefix sums + binary search
solutions.idea: The sorted prefix sums are increasing; the answer for a budget is how many of them are ≤ it.

followups: Prices can now be added and removed between queries. Which structure keeps the queries fast?
Each shopper must also take a specific item. How do you adjust the search?
